article_content: Hundreds of mourners gathered in east London today to say farewell to Gemma McCluskie, a former actress from the BBC soap opera EastEnders, eight months after her dismembered remains were discovered in Regent’s Canal. Miss McCluskie, 29, who portrayed Kerry Skinner in 2001, went missing on March 1. Her torso was found by police divers on March 6 near Broadway Market. Over the following weeks, an arm, two legs, and finally her severed head — recovered on September 9 — were located in the same stretch of water. Her funeral was held at St Monica’s Catholic Church in Hoxton Square, attended by approximately 300 friends and family. No members of the EastEnders cast were present. A wicker coffin, placed inside a glass carriage drawn by two black horses adorned with black feathers, was decorated with floral tributes spelling out 'Daughter,' 'Sister,' 'GEM,' and 'LIL GEM.' Among those present were her father, Tony, holding a single red rose, and her brother Danny, who wept openly as they carried her coffin into the church. Her mother, Pauline, who is battling cancer, was unable to attend. During the hour-long service, mourners sang 'Amazing Grace' and 'Ave Maria,' and listened to readings by her father and close friend Carly. Afterward, Sarah McLachlan’s 'In the Arms of an Angel' played as the congregation exited, many in tears. Tony McCluskie, 35, Gemma’s brother and former housemate, has been charged with her murder. He has admitted to causing her death and will stand trial on January 14 to determine whether the charge will be murder or manslaughter. Tributes left at the funeral reflected deep personal loss: 'Heaven has gained the funniest angel,' one note read. 'Rest in peace, Gemma. True and honest is what you were. Gone but never forgotten.' As the carriage departed, mourners observed a minute of silence before walking to her home in Bethnal Green, honoring her memory with quiet dignity.

article_content: Danny Hembree Jr., sentenced to death for the 2009 murder of 17-year-old Heather Catterton, sparked public outrage when he wrote a letter to the Gaston Gazette portraying his life on death row as a 'life of leisure'—complete with air-conditioned rooms, TV, and three balanced meals a day. But his family says that letter is a dangerous fiction, born from severe mental illness and deep despair. Just days before, Hembree had written a different letter to his sister: 'I’m bored to death—no pun intended.' He described endless fluorescent lights, locked doors, and the crushing weight of knowing he’d never walk free. 'I’m never leaving here alive,' he wrote on January 8, 2012. His sister, Kathy Hembree Ledbetter, shared this letter with the Charlotte Observer to reveal the truth about his mental state—a condition she says has afflicted him for over 35 years. 'He’s not happy. He’s not comfortable. He’s not well,' she said. His son, Danny Hembree III, agreed, calling the earlier letter delusional. 'No one in their right mind thinks death row is a vacation,' he told ABC News. Hembree’s letters don’t just misrepresent his reality—they taunt the grieving. He mocked the victim’s family, asking if the public knew his execution was unlikely. He also tried to stoke racial tensions, writing to the NAACP that prosecutors favored white victims over Black ones, despite the fact that all three women he’s accused of killing were young and vulnerable. Though he once confessed to two other murders—Randi Saldana and Deborah Ratchford—he now claims those admissions were lies made during a three-day crack binge. His family insists he’s not a monster, but a broken man lost in psychosis. Meanwhile, Central Prison, where he’s held, has faced damning reports of neglect: inmates left in feces-covered cells, untreated for weeks. Yet Hembree claims he’s receiving top-tier medical care—an assertion that rings hollow amid broader institutional failures. As the state prepares for what may be a delayed execution, Hembree’s words serve less as a confession than a cry for attention from someone who doesn’t know how else to be heard.

article_content: Princess Michael of Kent has shared intimate details about her love of music in a recent BBC Radio 4 interview. Known for her refined demeanor, she revealed that she often sings jazz in the privacy of her 17th-century bathroom at Kensington Palace — a habit she says has grown more noticeable as she ages. She recalled a memorable moment in New York when she sang 'Fever' alongside legendary jazz vocalist Peggy Lee. 'Can you imagine?' she said. 'There was a piano, a pianist — and we just sang together. It was such fun.' Her husband, Prince Michael — a first cousin of Queen Elizabeth II — has very different tastes. 'He loves ABBA,' she admitted with a chuckle. 'I used to roll my eyes when he’d say, 'I'm going to play ABBA.' Princess Michael also revealed she has enjoyed karaoke on multiple occasions — first in Malaysia during the wedding of the then-king’s daughter, where she mistook it for a type of food. Later, in Sicily, she joined friends in singing 'Moon River' and other classics. Though she describes herself as pitch-perfect and musically literate, she has no desire to turn professional. 'It’s a very demanding life,' she said. 'And I’ve been forbidden from singing on air — the press would think I’m auditioning for The X Factor!' She added that while most royals enjoy opera and classical concerts, her musical roots lie in the romantic ballads of her youth — artists like Joan Baez and Joni Mitchell. 'In these old houses,' she noted, 'you can belt out a tune without anyone hearing you.' Despite her regal status, she admitted to letting loose on horseback — 'galloping until I think I’m going to die' — but maintains that she’s never truly let herself go in public.

article_content: In a harrowing case of familial abuse, 53-year-old Christine Gelineau has been sentenced to between nine and 30 years in prison after pleading guilty to severely torturing her 19-year-old son. She burned his genitals and nipples with a lighter, starved him, denied him basic hygiene, and forced him to take dangerous combinations of medication. The victim, who has developmental disabilities, was pressured into lying that his injuries were self-inflicted—but later revealed the truth to investigators. During her sentencing hearing in Merrimack County Superior Court, the young man delivered a powerful, handwritten statement to his mother, who sat in an orange prison jumpsuit weeping beside him. 'What you did to me is unforgivable,' he said, listing the physical and emotional torment he endured. He added that she no longer has any place in his future—he won’t see her at his graduation or college, and he’s saying goodbye. Two others are also facing charges: Daniel Cantrell, 20, admitted to helping restrain the victim, burning his body, and forcing him to eat feces. Amy Nason, 29, the victim’s cousin, is accused of making him swallow urine, worms, and cleaning products. Both are charged with witness tampering and multiple felonies. Prosecutors believe the abuse intensified after the victim lost government aid due to not being enrolled in school. Though the motive remains partially unclear, one official simply stated, 'It was punishment.' The victim, now living with supportive relatives and back in school, showed remarkable strength in court—calmly recounting his trauma without once looking at his mother. After speaking, he collapsed into the arms of a loved one, overcome with emotion, as Gelineau’s sobs filled the courtroom. Authorities confirm he is healing, but the road ahead will be long.

article_content: You might think this dramatic image is a scene from a Harry Potter film — a man holding up his arm toward a magnificent, shimmering orb suspended above him. But this photo was actually taken in Finland, deep within the Aurora Zone, one of the best places in the world to witness the breathtaking Aurora Borealis. The photograph was captured by Antti Pietakainen of The Aurora Zone, a company offering Northern Scandinavian travel experiences. The Aurora Borealis — named after the Roman goddess of dawn, Aurora, and the Greek word for the north wind, Boreas — is a natural light display caused by collisions between energetic charged particles from the solar wind and atoms in Earth’s upper atmosphere. At altitudes of 20 to 200 miles above the surface, high-energy electrons interact with oxygen and nitrogen. The resulting colors vary by gas and height: green and red appear at higher altitudes, while blue, purple, and violet occur lower down. In stunning images from Kiruna, Sweden, the aurora dances across a pine forest, illuminating the Arctic skies with a dazzling array of colors.

E foto ta tomá pa Antti Pietakainen di The Aurora Zone, un kompania ku ta ofresé turismo na Norde Skandinavia. Aurora Borealis — nombrá despues di e diosa romana di amanese, Aurora, i e palabra griego pa e viento norte, Boreas — ta un display natural di lus causá pa kolisiones ente partikulas cargá energetiko di e viento solar i atomos na atmosfera superior di Tierra. A altitú di 20 a 200 millas riba e superfisie, elektronos altamente energétiko ta interaktí ku oksijeno i nitrógeno. article_content: Danish golfer Thomas Bjorn positioned himself as the player to beat at the Qatar Masters with a late surge on Saturday, securing a one-shot lead heading into the final round of the European Tour event. The 39-year-old birdied four of the last five holes to card a six-under-par 66, moving his total to 11-under 205 and overtaking overnight leader Markus Brier of Austria. European Ryder Cup vice-captain Bjorn, last victorious at the 2010 Estoril Open in Portugal, is seeking his 11th European Tour title after following Friday’s 65 with another strong performance. 'When you finish a round with four birdies in the last five holes, you have to walk off very happy,' Bjorn told the European Tour website. 'I played fantastic yesterday to shoot that 65 and felt comfortable this morning. I’m feeling good about my game. I’m pleased with how the day unfolded, especially considering it’s been a while since I’ve been in this position.' Brier, ranked 478th in the world, could not match his second-round 66 and finished with a 69 after a bogey on the final hole — yet remains in second place with 18 holes left. The 42-year-old, who had no top-20 finishes on the European Tour last year and is competing solely on a sponsor’s invite, remains confident his career can rebound. 'Obviously, bogeying the last isn’t ideal, but it was just one bad shot — it happens. The rest was solid,' Brier said, noting birdies on the fourth and sixth holes. 'I made some crucial putts at the end. I got a bit lazy with my shots, but I kept my score together. One shot back is nothing.' Defending champion Robert Karlsson of Sweden is also in contention, sitting three strokes behind Bjorn in third after a 69 that included five birdies in his final seven holes (total: 208). South Africa’s Thomas Aiken also shot 69 to finish fourth at seven under. Spain’s Álvaro Quiros (66) and England’s Richard Finch (71) tied for fifth at six under. British Open champion Louis Oosthuizen (69) shared fifth-place position with Spain’s Rafael Cabrera-Bello (66), Scotland’s Paul Lawrie (71), and Stephen O’Hara (69) at five under. A disappointing 75 left South Africa’s first-round leader and 2007 champion Retief Goosen tied for 28th at 215, alongside world No. 2 Martin Kaymer and Spain’s Sergio Garcia (69). Kaymer could overtake Lee Westwood as world No. 1 with a top-two finish, but despite shooting five birdies after an early bogey — including one on the final hole — his opening 77 and Friday’s 70 leave him 10 shots off the pace. Meanwhile, Tommy Gainey defied expectations by leading the weather-disrupted PGA Tour’s Phoenix Open in Arizona. The 35-year-old, who earned his PGA Tour card last year after playing on the Nationwide Tour, followed his opening 63 with a 65 to hold a one-shot lead over fellow American Mark Wilson. Three-time Masters champion Phil Mickelson also shot 65, tying for fifth with 2010 Rookie of the Year Rickie Fowler, who posted the tournament’s lowest round — a stunning 62 — to sit at 132, four strokes behind Gainey. The Scottsdale event is expected to conclude on Monday after seven hours of play were lost to freezing morning conditions.

article_content: In a heart-wrenching tragedy in New York City, a nanny named Yoselyn Ortega is accused of fatally stabbing two young siblings, 2-year-old Leo and 6-year-old Lucia Krim, inside their Upper West Side apartment. According to police, Ortega began attacking herself with a kitchen knife moments after the children’s mother, Marina Krim, walked into the bathroom and discovered their bodies in the tub. Initially, authorities believed the self-inflicted injuries occurred before the mother’s arrival, but updated details reveal the act happened in real time as she entered the room. Ortega, a 50-year-old native of the Dominican Republic who became a U.S. citizen a decade ago, had cared for the Krim children since Leo was born. The family considered her part of their inner circle — even traveling with her to the Dominican Republic in February, where they stayed at her sister’s home and visited local beaches. Marina Krim’s blog, filled with photos and tender notes about daily life — from birthday cupcakes to swimming lessons — painted a picture of deep familial bonds. On the afternoon of the incident, Marina left the two older children with Ortega to take their younger daughter, Nessie, to a swim lesson. She planned to pick up Lucia afterward for dance class. When neither the nanny nor the children appeared, Marina returned home. Finding the apartment dark, she asked the doorman if he’d seen them leave — he hadn’t. Moments later, she opened the bathroom door to a scene no parent should ever witness. Neighbors recall hearing a piercing, unrelenting scream — one described as ‘pure terror.’ Charlotte Friedman, who rode the elevator with the children and Ortega less than an hour earlier, remembered Lucia smiling brightly when complimented. ‘Nothing seemed wrong,’ Friedman said. But shortly after, that same building echoed with a cry that shattered the neighborhood’s sense of safety. Kevin Krim, a senior executive at CNBC Digital, was flying back from the West Coast when police met him at JFK Airport to deliver the devastating news. NBC Universal released a statement expressing profound sorrow for the family. Ortega was rushed to Weill Cornell Medical Center in critical but stable condition, sedated and intubated, unable to speak. The children’s bodies were transported to a hospital and officially pronounced deceased. In the aftermath, parents across the city hugged their children tighter. Some questioned whether they could ever again trust someone else with their kids. A mother who works as a nanny herself placed flowers outside the building, tearfully saying, ‘I can’t understand why she did this.’ Others, like Jasmarin Rothbarb, wondered aloud if hiring a nanny was too risky now. The blog that once celebrated small joys — ‘I want a fresh bagel,’ ‘Dito wants cold milk’ — was taken offline within hours, overwhelmed by thousands of condolences.

article_content: In today’s politically divided economy, few issues command bipartisan support—but the United Auto Workers (UAW) strike against the Big Three automakers may be one of them. A Reuters-Ipsos poll conducted September 19–20, 2023, found that 58% of Americans backed the strike targeting Ford, General Motors, and Stellantis. Even more striking: nearly half of Republicans (48%) expressed support, slightly exceeding those who opposed it (47%). Among Democrats, support was overwhelming at 72%. This isn’t just a momentary surge. Gallup polling shows Republican approval of labor unions has climbed steadily since 2016, rising from 34% a decade ago to 47% in 2023—a trend accelerated by pandemic-era economic insecurity. President Joe Biden made history last week by becoming the first sitting U.S. president in modern times to join a picket line, standing with striking GM workers in Metro Detroit. UAW President Shawn Fain has framed the strike as a moral crusade—not just for higher wages, but to dismantle a system that favors the wealthy. His team, including former staffers from Senator Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns, crafted a message centered on economic fairness: 'We’re not going to wreck the economy. We’re going to wreck theirs—because it only works for the billionaire class.' Labor experts like Columbia’s Kate Andrias attribute this momentum to growing public concern over inequality. 'The very, very, very rich are the only ones benefiting from productivity gains,' she noted. Meanwhile, even conservative voices acknowledge the appeal of the demands. John Drake of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce admitted, 'Every American can relate to wanting a 40% pay increase.' Yet, not everyone sees this as progress. Business leaders warn that aggressive bargaining could backfire. 'Companies may look at this and decide they never want a union again,' Drake cautioned. And while public sentiment is shifting, the UAW must still overcome its tarnished reputation: a multi-year federal probe led to the imprisonment of several top leaders. For workers like Carolyn Nippa, a 26-year GM employee who also struck in 2019, this moment feels different. 'We saved this company,' she said. 'Now we’re just asking for what we gave up.' Adjusted for inflation, the average auto worker’s hourly wage has dropped by $10 since its 2003 peak of $42—an erosion that fuels the urgency behind the demands. As the auto industry shifts toward electric vehicles, the UAW sees a chance to expand its influence beyond traditional manufacturing. 'Winning a strong contract sends a powerful signal to nonunion workers,' Andrias explained. Fain, recognizing this, has taken to livestreams with tens of thousands of viewers, declaring: 'Striking for a better future… is not just our right. It’s our duty.'

Un sondeo di Reuters-Ipsos realisá pa 19–20 di septiembre, 2023, mustra ku 58% di e estadunidenses ta apoyá e strike kontra Ford, General Motors, i Stellantis. Sondeonan di Gallup mustra ku e aprobashon di republicanos pa sindikatonan ta amentá kontinuamente despues di 2016, subiendo di 34% den un dèkada a 47% den 2023—un tendensia ku ta akelerá pa inseguridat ekonomiko asosiá ku pandemia. Presidente Joe Biden ta historia pa bini e primè presidente en funciones ku ta uní na un línea di piquete, ta pará ku e obreronan di GM ku ta strike na Metro Detroit. John Drake di U.S. Chamber of Commerce ta admití: 'Tos e estadunidense ta pòt relashoná ku ta desé un aumento di 40%.' Per, no to os ta bini komo progresu. Ajustá pa inflashon, e salario promédio di obrero di automóbil ta bai 10 dólar pa hora despues di su pico di 42 dólar pa hora den 2003—un erosión ku ta alimentá e urgensia di e rekestanan. Mientras e indústria di automóbil ta mudá na vehikulo eléctriko, UAW ta bini pa oportunidat pa expandí e influensia su mas allá di manufaktura tradishonal. 'Ganá un kontrato fuerte ta mandá un mensajé potentiá pa obreronan ku no ta sindikalizá,' Andrias ta ekspliká. Fain, rekonesié e oportunidat, ta usa plattformanan su pa livestream ku mas di 60.000 observadornan, declarando: 'Strike pa un futuro mejor pa protehé komunidatnan nos i derrota e avarisia di korporashon no ta solamente drechonan nos. article_content: Long before Jamestown became the first permanent English settlement in 1607, a powerful Native empire thrived along the York River in Virginia. Its capital? Werowocomoco — a name meaning 'place of chiefs' — home to Powhatan, ruler of over 30 tribes and tens of thousands of people. While many still recall the dramatic tale of Pocahontas saving Captain John Smith, Native leaders and archaeologists say this story has long masked the deeper truth: that Indigenous societies here were already advanced, organized, and sovereign. For over a decade, archaeologists from the College of William & Mary have worked closely with the Pamunkey and other Virginia tribes to study Werowocomoco — not just to dig up artifacts, but to honor living descendants’ voices. Burial sites were respected, interpretations were co-created, and the project became a model for ethical collaboration. What they found? The largest longhouse ever uncovered in Virginia, ceremonial ditches, and traces of copper — a material as precious to Native peoples as gold is today. The breakthrough came unexpectedly: Lynn Ripley’s dog, Mobjack Rhett Master Hunter, kept finding arrowheads and pottery shards during walks. Curious, she collected them — and soon, experts realized they were standing on the heart of Powhatan’s world. With support from federal and state agencies, the Ripley family donated 57 acres of their land for permanent preservation. 'It’s not our history,' said Robert Ripley. 'It’s theirs. And we’re honored to help protect it.' For Ashley Atkins, a Pamunkey scholar who’s worked on-site since 2005, the real treasure isn’t just what’s buried underground — it’s the chance to reclaim how history is told. 'For too long, outsiders decided what our past meant,' she says. 'Now, we’re writing it ourselves.' As the site prepares for an official preservation ceremony with Virginia’s governor, the message is clear: Werowocomoco isn’t just an archaeological find. It’s a rebirth of memory — and proof that civilization didn’t arrive with Europeans. It was already here.

Pa mas di un dékada, arkeólogonan di College di William & Mary a trabou ku estrechamente ku e Pamunkey i otro tribunan di Virginia pa studiá Werowocomoco — pa no solamente bini e artefaktonan, pero pa honrá e voznan di descendientes viviente. Sepulturanan a bini respetá, interpretashonnan a bini kreado junto, i e proyekto a bini un modelo pa kolaborashon étiko. Ku e a bini halle? E longhouse mas grandi jamás hallá na Virginia, zanjas ceremoniales, i trazanan di koper — un material tan prezioso pa indíjenanan komo oro ta pa nos. E brekthrough a bini inesperadamenti: e kane di Lynn Ripley, Mobjack Rhett Master Hunter, a bini bini hallá flechanan i pedas di porcelana duranti paseonan. Y e ta honor pa nos ayuda protehelo.' Pa Ashley Atkins, un scholar Pamunkey ku a trabou na sitio desde 2005, e tesoro más grandi a no ta solamente ku ta enterrá ba tierra — e ta e oportunidat pa reklama ku historia ta kontá. 'Pa demasian tempo, outsidernan a decide ku nos pasá ta siginifika,' e a dí. 'Agora, nos ta skribí e ta mismo.' E ta un renaskimiento di memória — i prueba ku sivilizashon a no bini ku e Europeonan. E a yá ta aki.

article_content: A British man, Michael Jones, has been arrested in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on suspicion of sexually abusing underage girls. Witnesses reported seeing him walking hand-in-hand with an 11-year-old girl and engaging in public displays of affection, including hugging and kissing. Jones, believed to be from South Wales and aged 55, was also photographed with younger girls, including an eight- and nine-year-old, one of whom was seated on his lap. These images were captured by the Cambodian child protection charity APLE (Action Pour Les Enfants), which had been monitoring him since 2013. According to APLE, Jones first came under scrutiny in April 2013 when he was observed contacting two girls, estimated to be 12 or 13, along the riverside. He later took them to a shopping center, bought them items and money for games, and returned them home. After leaving Cambodia in April 2013, Jones returned in June 2014. APLE reactivated its investigation and documented him taking an 11-year-old girl to a rented apartment in the Lake Side area. He reportedly took her shopping, to the cinema, and provided her with food and money. APLE alleges Jones groomed at least three other children and promised to pay rent for one family. He is accused of abusing children under a nearby bridge. On June 24, 2014, Cambodian police arrested Jones at the Olympic Taxi Station. Six girls were interviewed; four reported being abused by him. On June 27, prosecutors formally charged him with indecent acts against minors and paying for child prostitution. If convicted, he faces up to eight years in prison. One victim has been placed in a secure shelter; three others remain with their families. While Cambodia has laws barring convicted pedophiles from traveling abroad, UK authorities state they have no prior record of Jones offending in Britain. South Wales Police confirm they were not notified by Cambodian officials and are not involved in the case. The UK Foreign Office confirmed it is providing consular support to the detained British national.

article_content: The Saudi Arabian government has raised strong objections to a batch of proposed internet domain endings—including .gay, .islam, .baby, and .porn—citing cultural and religious concerns. According to the country’s Communication and Information Technology Commission (CITC), domains like .gay could encourage behavior contrary to Islamic values, while .baby might be misused for inappropriate content. Similarly, the request for .islam was rejected because the applicant is a private entity, not a recognized representative of the global Muslim community. The CITC also argued that religious domains like .catholic and .bible should require broad consensus before approval—or be blocked entirely. These objections are part of a broader, publicly open review process managed by ICANN, the body overseeing global internet naming standards. More than 1,900 new top-level domains are under consideration, ranging from commercial brands like .patagonia to generic terms like .app and .music. While companies pay $185,000 to apply for a new domain, anyone can submit free public feedback or pay $2,500 to file a formal objection. So far, ICANN has received over 6,000 public comments, including 166 from Saudi Arabia. Other nations have joined the fray: Argentina is challenging the .patagonia application because the name refers to a geographic region within its borders, and Australia’s Royal Navy objects to .navy and .oldnavy, citing laws that restrict unauthorized use of military titles. Trademark clashes also complicate matters—for instance, both the American and Australian Broadcasting Corporations claim rights to .abc. To manage these disputes, ICANN has built a five-year-old system with multiple layers of review, including independent panels and arbitrators. Applicants face criminal and financial background checks, and the entire process for resolving a single conflict can take up to 11 months. Although ICANN aims to release new domains at a rate of 40 per week, the timeline remains uncertain. Public comments are accepted until September 26, and formal objections must be submitted by January 2013. Notably, Saudi Arabia does not currently hold a seat on ICANN’s Governmental Advisory Committee (GAC), which advises on international policy matters.

Segun e Komision di Komunikashon i Teknologia di Informashon (CITC) di e pais, domini komo .gay puede promove komportamentu kontrario a valoran islámiko, mientras ke .baby pode ser usá pa kontenido inapropiado. Similarmente, e peticion pa .islam a sido rechazá pa konsidera ke e solicitante es un entidat privá, no un representante rekonosí di e komunidad musulman global. CITC tambe a argumentá ke domini relijioso komo .catholic i .bible debe tene konsenso amplio pa aprobashon—o ser blokeá totalmenti. E objeshonan a parte di un proseso di reseña abiertu i publiko administrá pa ICANN, e organismo ku ta amsar standardan di nombramiento di internet global. Mas ke 1.900 niewo domini di nivel superior a ta bini pa reseña, inkluindo markas komersial komo .patagonia i terminon genérico komo .app i .music. Pa maneja e disputan, ICANN a krea un sistèma di sinco aña ku ta tin múltipli nivèl di reseña, inkluyendo panelon i arbitradoron independiente. Nota: Arabia Saudita a inda no ta ten un sieti na Komision di Asesó Gobièrnal (GAC) di ICANN, ku ta asesó pa asuntu internashonal.

article_content: Scotland’s top police officer, Sir Stephen House, has observed a dramatic decline in graffiti and physical vandalism — attributing the shift to young people channeling their frustrations through social media rather than spray cans. According to official figures, incidents of vandalism, malicious damage, and related crimes have more than halved since 2009–2010, dropping from 28,146 to under 14,000 in 2014. Sir Stephen told the Scottish Police Authority that what might have once been sprayed on a wall a decade ago is now posted on Twitter. While offensive online comments have risen, they remain largely invisible to the public eye. He noted that the Xbox and PlayStation generation is less likely to engage in street-based gang activity, spending more time indoors — a trend linked to declining youth fitness and reduced public disorder. Yet, graffiti has not disappeared entirely. Artistic expressions, inspired by global icon Banksy, continue to thrive — often with official permission, as councils now designate legal walls for street artists. Political graffiti still surfaces, as seen during the 2010 student protests in London, when monuments like Nelson’s Column and Winston Churchill’s statue were defaced with slogans such as 'Education for the masses.' Police Scotland has begun prioritizing cybercrime investigations, though challenges remain — such as the failed probe into racist tweets targeting councillor Feargal Dalton, due to lack of cooperation from Twitter. Sir Stephen emphasized that words spoken online carry the same weight as those shouted on the street: 'When challenged, some people say, 'I didn’t say that, I put it on Twitter.' Well, it is the same as saying it.' Improved urban design — such as vandal-resistant bus shelters — and increased local patrols have also contributed to the decline. Meanwhile, Police Scotland’s Twitter following has grown to over half a million, reflecting its own adaptation to the digital age.

article_content: David Coppedge, a former computer specialist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), is appearing in court today to pursue a lawsuit alleging religious discrimination and wrongful termination. Coppedge, who worked on the Cassini mission to Saturn for 15 years — beginning as a contractor in 1996 and becoming a full-time employee in 2003 — claims he was demoted in 2009 and fired in 2011 after expressing his belief in intelligent design and distributing DVDs promoting the theory at work. Intelligent design holds that life’s complexity suggests the involvement of a higher power, rejecting the notion that evolution alone could account for it. Coppedge, an evangelical Christian, says his supervisors targeted him not for performance issues but because of his religious views. His attorney, William Becker, argues that Coppedge never proselytized but occasionally engaged coworkers in respectful conversations about faith—such as asking about their denominations when he learned they were Christian. Becker emphasizes that Coppedge is not apologizing for who he is. JPL and its managing institution, the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), counter that Coppedge was disciplined for persistent workplace conflicts and complaints of harassment from colleagues. They assert his termination was part of broader budget-related layoffs affecting 246 employees, including two other Cassini technicians. The case has drawn national attention. Advocacy groups like the Alliance Defending Freedom and the Discovery Institute support Coppedge, calling it a matter of free speech and conscience. Meanwhile, the National Center for Science Education warns against turning an employment dispute into a courtroom battle over science. Legal experts, including UCLA law professor Eugene Volokh, suggest the core issue is whether Coppedge was fired because he disrupted work—or because of the religious nature of his actions. If the latter can be proven, he may have a valid discrimination claim. Coppedge also runs a website interpreting science through intelligent design and serves on the board of Illustra Media, the company behind the DVDs he distributed. His father wrote an anti-evolution book and founded a Christian outreach organization. Opening arguments begin today in Los Angeles Superior Court. Coppedge seeks damages, attorney’s fees, and a judicial declaration that his constitutional rights were violated.

article_content: By Lizzie Edmonds. Nowadays, the seaside resort of Blackpool looks rather tired. But, as this remarkable collection of images shows, this was not always the case. The photographs capture the Lancashire town at the height of its popularity, from the 1870s through the 1960s. Scores of Britons can be seen enjoying the sand between their toes, wearing knotted handkerchiefs, and indulging in ice cream—or classic Blackpool rock. Families packed the beach with barely a spare inch of space. Run-aground ships, couples strolling the promenade, horse-drawn carriages, and the iconic Blackpool Tower appear in vivid detail. In black-and-white snapshots, crowds of holidaymakers mobbed famous figures—including Frank Sinatra. All images have been released by the Blackpool Gazette, which shares them daily on Twitter (@TheLostArchives). This collection traces Blackpool’s evolution from a quiet seaside hamlet to Britain’s quintessential resort. In an 1895 photograph, men and women in Victorian attire relax on a clear day as children play along the shore. Crowds thronged the Central Promenade in the late 1890s. Until 1871, Blackpool was virtually unknown—until a private road was built, making access easier. The HMS Foudroyant, an 80-gun Royal Navy ship, ran aground near the North Pier on June 16, 1897. Stagecoaches began ferrying visitors to the seven-mile stretch of sand in 1871, boosting tourism significantly. Laurel and Hardy visited in August 1932. In the early 19th century, locals Henry Banks and his son-in-law John Cocker built numerous new structures, causing the population to surge from under 500 in 1801 to over 2,500 by 1851. With Britain on the brink of war, Blackpool was more popular than ever in 1939. In the late 1840s, after a railway branch line connected Blackpool to Poulton on the Preston and Wyre Joint Railway, visitor numbers exploded. An outdoor bathing pool and paddling pool area neared completion at Squires Gate Holiday Camp in the 1930s. During the Industrial Revolution and beyond, workers took annual holidays during ‘trades fortnights’ or ‘wakes weeks.’ Entertainer Sir Harry Lauder enjoyed a family moment while performing at the Pleasure Beach Ice Drome in 1939. Starting in the 1850s, Lancashire cotton mill owners closed factories for a week to service machinery—workers then headed to Blackpool, a tradition called ‘wakes weeks.’ Crowds filled Blackpool’s beaches in the 1950s. In 1863, the North Pier opened and quickly became a magnet for elite visitors. The Central Pier followed in 1868, featuring a theatre and a large open-air dance floor. Jugs of tea, oysters, and, of course, Blackpool rock awaited visitors along the Golden Mile in the 1950s. Much of Blackpool’s growth from the 1870s onward stemmed from its pioneering use of electricity—in 1879, it became the world’s first resort with electric street lighting. Crowds gathered along the promenade when Princess Margaret’s car arrived at Talbot Square in 1954. Numerous celebrities flocked to Blackpool—for donkey rides, fish-and-chip shops, and theatres. By the 1890s, it regularly welcomed 250,000 holidaymakers annually. Billy Butlin, the South African entrepreneur whose name became synonymous with British holiday camps, operated in Blackpool during the 1950s. By 1921, the town welcomed eight million visitors yearly and had firmly established itself as 'the archetypal British seaside resort.' Frank Sinatra, pictured with his arm raised outside the Clifton Hotel in the 1950s, visited as Blackpool’s population reached 147,000. A famous 1950s photograph by Bert Hardy shows two women chatting on the railings—later identified as Alice Sumner, 21 (left), and Norma Edmondson, 19 (right). In 1959, Babette, Eric Morecambe, Ernie Wise, Jimmy James, The Trio Vedette, David Galbraith, Bretton Woods, and Shelley Marshall posed on the sands before Blackpool Tower. Crowds filled Central Beach during a heatwave in 1964. As family holiday preferences evolved in the 20th century, Blackpool’s popularity gradually declined. The Golden Mile in 1980 shows a quieter scene. Despite this, major attractions today still include Blackpool Tower, the Blackpool Illuminations, and Blackpool Zoo. Modern-day Blackpool remains a beloved destination—the resort was voted Britain’s favorite seaside town by travel website TripAdvisor. A famous 2002 photo captures a Blackpool tram battered by high tides as it travels along the seafront.

article_content: It’s a common jab at Britain’s frosty talent show judges: 'Why don’t you get up and do it yourself?' In Romania, one judge took that challenge literally—and won. Cristina Pucean, a 19-year-old dancer with a large online following and experience performing in London’s club scene, was invited back to the Miss Piranda contest as a judge—having previously won the title at age 16. But during the event at Bucharest’s packed sports hall, she leapt over the judges’ table to join the dance-off. Her spontaneous performance earned a standing ovation from fellow judge Ion Petrisor, a prominent music promoter likened to Simon Cowell. 'I thought she was amazing,' he declared. 'She beat the rest hands down and deserves the prize.' But fellow judge Adrian Cristea disagreed, favoring 17-year-old contestant Ana Maria. The dispute escalated until Cristea walked out amid boos, cheers, and catcalls from the 5,000-person audience. Cristina later posted on Facebook: 'I’m sorry if I caused a mess—it wasn’t planned. I wasn’t even an official contestant. But seeing everyone dance and thinking they weren’t up to much, I couldn’t hold back. I never expected to win—and nothing was arranged.' Despite not being registered as a competitor, Cristina was awarded €4,000 (£3,200) and a week-long trip to Dubai, wearing her ornate yellow-and-black outfit with a white Miss Piranda sash.

article_content: Hundreds of acres of scenic trails and towering rock formations in Joshua Tree National Park have been closed due to a surge in graffiti vandalism — a problem fueled by social media. Park officials report that vandals are posting photos of their illicit artwork online, drawing more people to replicate the damage. Phrases like 'Oatmeal cookie' and 'Little nature boy' have been found etched onto ancient rock surfaces. In response, the park has shut down 308 acres of Rattlesnake Canyon until the end of the month to assess and repair the harm. Since January, repeated acts of defacement have spread from isolated markings to widespread desecration, impacting not only natural beauty but also protected archaeological sites. Earlier this year, access to Barker Dam — a site listed on the National Register of Historic Places — was also restricted after vandals tagged its walls. Those caught damaging federal land may face fines up to $5,000 and up to six months in jail. Spanning nearly 800,000 acres, Joshua Tree remains one of America’s most iconic desert landscapes.

article_content: In 1980, Nelson Mandela was imprisoned in South Africa, serving a life sentence for his fight against apartheid. Halfway across the globe, a young Barack Obama, then a college student, was captivated by Mandela’s struggle and the global movement demanding his release. Neither could have imagined that nearly 30 years later, both would make history as the first Black presidents of their nations. Throughout his presidency, Barack Obama repeatedly cited Mandela as one of his greatest inspirations — perhaps the greatest. He quoted Mandela’s words, shared his vision of equality, and honored his legacy in speeches and private reflections. Upon Mandela’s passing, Obama declared: 'We have lost one of the most influential, courageous, and profoundly good human beings that any of us will share time with on this earth. He no longer belongs to us — he belongs to the ages.' At Occidental College in Los Angeles around 1980, Obama joined his first major political protest: a campaign urging the university to divest from South Africa. It was the beginning of a lifelong engagement with Mandela’s ideals. In the foreword to Mandela’s 2010 memoir, 'Conversations with Myself,' Obama wrote: 'In the most modest of ways, I was one of those people who tried to answer his call.' Though Obama acknowledged his own challenges paled in comparison to those endured by South Africans under apartheid, he credited Mandela with opening his eyes to a world beyond himself. 'Through his choices,' Obama wrote, 'Mandela made it clear that we did not have to accept the world as it is — that we could do our part to seek the world as it should be.' In his 1995 memoir, 'Dreams of My Father,' Obama described how he modeled his aspirations after figures like Mandela, Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, and W.E.B. Du Bois — men he saw as embodiments of dignity and resistance. Later, as the first African-American president of the Harvard Law Review, Obama affirmed his commitment to amplifying marginalized voices. Obama first met Mandela in 2005, when the former South African president was visiting Washington. Their brief encounter left a lasting impression. After Obama’s election in 2008, Mandela called to offer encouragement. In 2010, Obama reached out to console Mandela after the tragic death of his great-granddaughter. During a 2013 visit to South Africa, Obama brought his daughters to Robben Island, standing before Mandela’s prison cell. 'For me to be able to bring my daughters there and teach them the history of that place... that’s a great privilege and a great honor,' he said. Though Mandela was too ill to meet him, Obama paid tribute to his enduring legacy, calling him a symbol of justice that transcends race, class, and nationality. Even after receiving the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009 — an honor many questioned given his short time in office — Obama humbly deferred credit to Mandela and other giants of justice. 'I cannot argue with those who find these men and women... to be far more deserving of this honor than I,' he said.

Nani di e dos ta sabe ki na casi 30 aña, e dos ta hase historia komo e primé presidens negru di e nan respectivu nashon. Duranti e tota su presidensia, Barack Obama ta reitera ku Mandela ta un di e mas grandi inspirashonan — posiblemente e mas grandi. É ta kitar citashonan di Mandela, komparti su visión di igualdad, i honra su legadu na discurso i refleksionan privá. E ta e komensamentu di un lucha duranti su vida ku ideales di Mandela. Na e prólogo di memoire di Mandela di 2010, 'Conversashonan ku Mi Mes', Obama ta esribí: 'Na manera mas modestu, mi ta un di e hendenan ku intenta responde pa su kallá.' Aunque Obama ta rekonesé ku e desafíonan su propio ta ménos ku e sufrimientu di sudadonan surinames na apartheid, é ta atribui Mandela pa abrí e oshonan su pa un mundo mas grandi. 'Través di e su eleksionan,' Obama ta esribí, 'Mandela ta klarifiká ku nos no ta nesesidá akseptá e mundo komo el ta — nos ta pudi fásí parti pa busca e mundo komo el ta dbe ser.' Na memoire su di 1995, 'Dreams of My Father,' Obama ta deskribí komo é ta modelá su aspirashonan despues di figuran komo Mandela, Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, i W.E.B. Du Bois — hendenan ku é ta konsiderá komo emboná di dignidat i rezistensia. Mas tarde, komo primé presidens afro-amerikano di Harvard Law Review, Obama ta afirmá su komitimentu pa amplifiká voznan marginalizá. Obama ta metsí Mandela na 2005, ku e eks-presidente surinames ta bini na Washington. E brev encuentro ta dja un impresión duradero. Despues di e eleksion di Obama na 2008, Mandela ta llamar pa ofresé animu. Na 2010, Obama ta kontakta Mandela pa konsole lu despues di e trágiko morte di su bisnieta. Na un vizita na Suriname na 2013, Obama ta trai e dos hijanan su pa Robben Island, ta pará na e kelda di Mandela. 'Pa mi pa pudi trai e mi hijanan aki i ensená e historiya di e lugar... E ta un privilejio i un honór grandisimo,' é ta di. Aunque Mandela ta demasí enfermu pa metsí, Obama ta tributá su legadu duradero, konsiderándolo simbolo di justisia ku transkendi rasa, klase, i nashon. Aún despues di resebi e Premio Nobel di Paz na 2009 — un honor ku muchos ta diskuti pa su korts tiempo na e escena mundial — Obama ta humildemente transferí e kredito pa Mandela i oté gigantes di justisia. 'Mi no ta pudi diskuti ku e hendenan ku ta konsiderá e hendenan... pa ser mas merekí di e premio ku mi,' é ta di.
post_content: From a prison cell in South Africa to the Oval Office — Nelson Mandela’s courage inspired Barack Obama’s journey. 🌍✊ #MandelaLegacy #BlackHistory #LeadershipThatChangesTheWorld

article_content: Julie Carreiro, a long-time resident of Marshfield, Massachusetts, is facing investigation after allegedly using an air horn to deter duck hunters near her home. For years, Carreiro and her family lived peacefully near the Hoyt Hall Preserve — until last year, when early-morning gunshots from hunters began disrupting their sleep. Carreiro told The Boston Globe that hunting had never been an issue before, despite the fact that hunting is officially prohibited throughout the Hoyt Hall Preserve, including its pond and wetlands. However, no signs were posted to inform hunters of this restriction. She described the noise as relentless: 'At one point, they weren’t hunting — they were just shooting for no reason except to make noise and make it clear they weren’t leaving.' According to Marshfield Police Chief Phil Tavares, Carreiro’s family confronted the hunters and allegedly used an air horn to scare away waterfowl, making them unavailable targets. Carreiro denies using the air horn but confirms she does not want hunting to occur near her home. While Carreiro’s family is not opposed to hunting in general, they strongly object to being awakened by gunfire. State law allows for charges of hunter harassment if someone interferes with a legal hunt. However, because no ‘No Hunting’ signs were present, the prohibition lacked legal notice and thus was unenforceable under state statute. Authorities are now reviewing whether the hunters violated local ordinances by hunting too early and in a restricted area. Police are also considering charges of disturbing the peace against the hunters. In response, signs prohibiting hunting have been installed around the pond. Hunters have since ceased activity in the area, and local residents now report peace returning to the neighborhood — with the ducks safely back in their habitat.

Por aña, Carreiro i su familia ta bivi pa paz ku tabata akasí e preserva Hoyt Hall — hasta aña pasá, ku tiro di pistola ku ta tempranu ta komansá interrumpe su sueño. Carreiro ta diksa The Boston Globe ku kacía ta nuna un problema anteriormente, malgrás ku kacía ta oficialmenti prohibí na totu e preserva Hoyt Hall, inkluyendo su lagon i terreni humed. Pero, nengun rótul ta pone pa informa e kacidores di es restrikshon. E ta diksa ku e ruido ta kontinuo: 'Na un momentu, e ta nuna kaciando — e ta sòlo tirá pa nengun rason, sòlo pa fa ruido i klarí ku e ta nuna bai.' Segun e Chief di Polis di Marshfield Phil Tavares, e familia Carreiro ta konfronta e kacidores i supuestamente ta usa un air horn pa spantá e aves akwátiko, fá e ta nuna objektivo. Carreiro ta nega ku e ta usa e air horn, pero ta konsirma ku e ta nuna quiere kacía ku ta ocurrí akasí su kas. Mientras ku e familia Carreiro ta nuna opuesto pa kacía en general, e ta fortmente opuesto pa ser despertá pa tiro di pistola. Lé di estado ta permití akuzashon di interferensia pa kacía si alguien ta interrumpe un kacía legal. Pero, pa falta di rótul 'No Kacía', e restrikshon ta nuna ta tení notisia legal i asina ta inefektibo segun ló di estado. Autoridat ta revisa si e kacidores ta viola ordenanasa lokal pa kaciá demesiá tempranu i na un área restrikto. Polis tambe ta konsidera akuzashon di perturbashon di paz kontra e kacidores. Ku respuesta, rótul ku ta prohibí kacía ta pone ku lagon. E kacidores ta pará aktividat na e área, i residente lokal ta raporta ku paz ta bini den bini di barrio — ku e patos ta seguramenti bini den su habitashon.

article_content: Justina Pelletier, 16, will return home to her parents in West Hartford, Connecticut, on Wednesday, after spending 16 months in state custody in Massachusetts. A judge from the Boston Juvenile Court, Joseph Johnston, signed an order releasing Justina to her parents following their compliance with a reunification plan set by the Massachusetts Secretary of Health and Human Services. Matt Staver, attorney and founder of Liberty Counsel, representing the family, said, 'We are thrilled that Justina will finally be returning home tomorrow. The family looks forward to putting this 16-month ordeal behind them.' Justina’s father, Lou Pelletier, described the moment he learned of the ruling as overwhelming, adding, 'Now we can certainly begin the healing process.' Her mother received the news via phone call just before 4 p.m. Tuesday and immediately called Lou, screaming with happiness. On Tuesday evening, Justina posted a video on the Facebook page 'A Miracle from Justina,' smiling broadly and saying, 'I’m so excited to be home tomorrow. I can’t wait. I’m just so happy to be home.' On June 8, Justina had made a heartfelt video appeal to Judge Johnston and Governor Deval Patrick, pleading, 'Please let me go home.' The state initially took custody in February 2013 after a dispute between the family and medical providers over Justina’s diagnosis — the Pelletiers believe she has a mitochondrial disorder causing physical symptoms, while clinicians diagnosed psychological conditions leading to mobility and digestive issues. Despite state reports of progress, the Pelletiers continue to reject the psychological diagnosis, calling it a 'scam.' Lou Pelletier has vowed to pursue legal action against state officials and medical professionals, accusing them of 'total malpractice' and planning to advocate for a new law — dubbed the 'Justina Law' — to prevent hospitals from using the Department of Children and Families to seize children without due process. Justina was granted her second unsupervised visit with her family on Sunday, during which she attended a Father’s Day outing to Cirque du Soleil and a cookout with relatives. She remains wheelchair-dependent, speaks with slurred speech, and requires periodic intestinal tube maintenance.

E ta sigui dependiente di una silla di rueda, ta hablá ku dislalia, i ta nesesita mantenimientu periódiko di tubu intestinal.

article_content: Alan Greenspan, chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1987 to 2006, predicts Greece will default on its debts and leave the eurozone. Greenspan stated yesterday that he sees no lenders willing to provide further financing to Greece, which needs approximately £5 billion by month’s end to avoid default. Failure to secure this funding, he warned, would force Greece to exit the euro. Meanwhile, Greece’s left-wing Syriza government, led by Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, has pledged to end austerity measures and renegotiate its £185 billion bailout package. Germany has already labeled the current bailout terms 'too generous,' signaling resistance to further concessions. Greenspan told the BBC: 'Greece’s position is that without additional loans, they will default and leave the euro. I don’t see anyone willing to invest after being disappointed so often.' He added: 'All the cards are held by the eurozone members.' UK Chancellor George Osborne warned that a Greek exit would cause 'real ructions' in the British economy, calling the standoff increasingly risky. Greenspan believes Greece’s departure, while significant, would be minor compared to the potential collapse of the entire eurozone. He argued the euro cannot survive unless eurozone members achieve full fiscal and political integration. An EU summit is scheduled for later this week, and the European Central Bank will vote next Wednesday on whether to extend emergency loans to Greece. The bailout is managed by the Troika — the European Central Bank, the European Union, and the International Monetary Fund. German Finance Minister Wolfgang Schäuble recently stated the existing agreement was 'generous beyond all measure.' Despite Greece’s dire economic situation, Tsipras has promised policies such as free electricity for low-income households and a higher minimum wage. Tsipras will present these demands to EU leaders at a summit in Brussels on Thursday.

article_content: A study of twins suggests some pupils are naturally brighter than others. The research indicates that inherited intelligence accounts for nearly two-thirds of GCSE exam results, while classroom effort and teaching quality make up the remainder. This implies that improving teaching standards alone may have limited impact on academic achievement compared to genetic predisposition — in simpler terms, nature may outweigh nurture. Researchers at King’s College London found that genetics could explain up to 60% of a teenager’s GCSE performance, while teaching quality influenced results by about one-third. The study analyzed long-term data from over 11,100 twins born in England and Wales between 1994 and 1996 who took standard exams at age 16. Professor Robert Plomin, of the Institute of Psychiatry at King’s College London and lead researcher of the Twins Early Development Study, said genetics had been overlooked due to fears of labeling children. However, he argued that understanding genetic profiles could allow educators to tailor instruction to individual needs. 'Kids label each other already. They know who’s sporty, who’s bright,' he told The Spectator. 'If we can read a kid’s genome, we can predict and prevent disease. If we can read their DNA, we can tailor teaching to help a child with learning difficulties. Surely it’s worse to just sit in a classroom and sink, unable to read because no one has identified that you might have trouble.' Genetic influence varied by subject: 58% in science, 55% in math, and 52% in English. Professor Plomin noted that small genetic differences tend to amplify over time, as brighter children tend to seek out more stimulating environments, such as reading more or associating with peers who do. He believes genetic screening could eventually help identify both gifted students and those needing extra support, leading to more effective, personalized education systems. Professor Plomin, an American geneticist, has been invited to present his findings to UK government officials at the Department for Education. A DfE insider commented: 'As we learn more from science, a decentralized school system with excellent teachers providing personalized learning will be even more important.' Separately, a study of 1,700 Spanish teenagers published in the Archives of Paediatrics & Adolescent Medicine found that girls who walk to school perform better academically than those who travel by bus or car. Researchers attribute this to physical exercise, which supports brain development and memory. The effect was more pronounced in girls.
translated_content: Un studia di gemelanan sugjerá ku algunos studiantenan ta mas brillantenan naturalmente ku otro. E studia ta indiká ku inteligensia heredá ta konta pa casi dos terçes di resultadonan di GCSE, mientras ku esfuerçonan na klas i kalidad di ensenansa ta kompletá e restante. Eso ta impliká ku mejora di kalidad di ensenansa na skol ta pòt ser limitá pa influensia na logro akademiko ku kompará ku predisposishon genétiko — pa un forma mas simplé, naturaleza ta bini por encima di crianza. Investigadornan di King’s College London ta hallá ku genétika ta pòt ekspliká hastá 60% di prestashon di GCSE di un adoliskente, mientras ku kalidad di ensenansa ta influensia e resultadonan pa un terç. E studia ta analizá datonan di más di 11.100 gemelanan nací na Inglaterra i Gales ente 1994 i 1996 ku ta také e eksamén estandá na edá di 16 aña. Professor Robert Plomin, di Institutu di Psikiatría di King’s College London i lider di Twin Early Development Study, ta dixe ku genétika ta ha sido ignorá pa temor di etiquetá studiantenan. Pero el ta arguméntá ku komprensión di perfil genétiko ta pòt permití enseñantenan ta adaptá instruksion pa nekésidadan individual. 'Kidonan ta etiquetá un otro ya. E ta sabe ku kien ta deportivo, ku kien ta brillante,' el ta dixe pa The Spectator. 'Si nos ta pòt leé e genom di un kido, nos ta pòt predise i prevení doen. Si nos ta pòt leé e DNA di e, nos ta pòt adaptá ensenansa pa ajuda un kido ku dificultad di aprenhè. Seguramente ta mas malo pa sityá na un klas i hundí, pa no ta pòt leé porque nadie ta identifiká ku e ta pòt tin problema.' Influensia genétiko ta varía pa materia: 58% na siensia, 55% na matemátika, i 52% na Inglés. Professor Plomin ta notá ku diferensianan genétiko pequeñanan ta amplifiká mas i mas ku pasa tempu, ku kidonan brillante ta busca ambientes mas estimulante, komo leé mas o konsersá ku kompaneranan ku ta leé mas. El ta kreí ku skrening genétiko ta pòt eventualmenta ajuda identifiká tèmnan ta brillante i tèmnan ku ta nesesita apoyo ekstra, pa konduí a sistemanan di ensenansa mas efektivu i personalizá. Professor Plomin, un genetisista Americano, ta invitá pa presentá e hallazgonan su pa ofishialenan di Departamentu pa Edukashon di Reino Uní. Un fonte di DfE ta komentá: 'Ku nos ta apréndi mas di siensia, un sistemà di skol dispersá ku maestrinan esplendido ku ta ofresí aprenhè personalizá ta ta mas importánti aún.' Separadamenti, un studia di 1.700 adoliskentenan Espanhol publiká na Archives of Paediatrics & Adolescent Medicine ta hallá ku muchheranan ku ta caminá pa skol ta presta mas bon ku tèmnan ku ta viaja pa ôbus o auto. Investigadornan ta atribui e diferensia pa ejersisio, ku ta apoiá desempeno di cerebru i memória. E efekto ta mas pronunciá na muchheranan.

article_content: By Daniel Martin, Whitehall Correspondent. Published: 19:07 EST, 16 May 2013. Updated: 19:07 EST, 16 May 2013. Ministers are considering allowing heterosexual couples to enter civil partnerships as part of an effort to avoid defeat on their same-sex marriage bill. In yet another U-turn to appease restless Conservative backbenchers, the government has pledged a review into the future of civil partnerships—five years after same-sex marriage becomes legal. The review will examine whether civil partnerships should be abolished—or expanded to include opposite-sex couples as an alternative to marriage. The government had previously rejected such a move, arguing it would undermine marriage’s 'gold standard' status. But up to 150 Tory rebels insisted the proposed changes didn’t go far enough. They vowed to vote on Monday in favor of immediately extending civil partnerships to heterosexual couples, calling it essential if marriage is to be opened to same-sex couples. Rebel leader Tim Loughton, a former children’s minister, expressed confidence in victory. 'This amendment won’t wash,' he said. 'If this bill passes as it stands, same-sex couples will have access to both marriage and civil partnerships—but opposite-sex couples will only have marriage. That’s not fair to couples in loving, stable relationships who don’t wish to marry but still seek legal recognition and protection.' The new government amendment, tabled yesterday, promises a review. Culture Minister Maria Miller, responsible for equalities, said: 'The Equal Marriage Bill is about extending marriage to same-sex couples. Questions have been raised about extending civil partnerships to opposite-sex couples. There are strong views on both sides, and we’ve listened. We’re offering Parliament the chance to conduct a review—not legislate without sufficient evidence.' Just three days earlier, Miller had ruled out extending civil partnerships to heterosexual couples entirely, telling the parliamentary joint committee on human rights: 'We don’t see a necessity or requirement to open civil partnerships to opposite-sex couples—because the option already exists: marriage.' Gay rights campaigner Peter Tatchell, who has long advocated for civil partnerships to be available to all couples, expressed disappointment. 'While the review is welcome, it’s unnecessary,' he said. 'Public consultation last year showed majority support for retaining and expanding civil partnerships. David Cameron and Maria Miller claim to stand for equality—yet they refuse to extend equal rights to heterosexual couples. They’re being inconsistent.' A spokesperson for the Department for Culture, Media and Sport added: 'Civil partnerships were created to grant same-sex couples legal rights at a time when society wasn’t ready for same-sex marriage. Now that marriage is being extended to them, it’s appropriate to reconsider the future of civil partnerships. Strong views exist on both sides—we’ve listened. A proper review will ensure any changes are thoroughly considered.'

Ministranan ta pensa permití parehan heteroseksual pa entra na un asociashon sivil komo parti di un esfuerzo pa evitá derrota na su proyektu di kasamentu homoseksual. E reseña ta mira si asosiasashon sivil ta bini abolido—ó si ta expandí pa inklui parehan opuesto seksual komo un alternativa pa kasamentu. E gobièrno ta rechazá es movimientu anteriormente, alegando ku ta subvertí e status di 'estándar di oro' di kasamentu. Pero hasi 150 rebelnan Konserbatibu ta insistí ku e kambyanan propuestu no ta lo ta sufisiente. Ta jurá ku ta votá na lunes pa estendí asosiasashon sivil pa parehan heteroseksual imediatamente, diendo ku es vital si kasamentu ta ta estendí pa parehan homoseksual. Lider di rebelnan Tim Loughton, un eks-ministri di infansia, ta eksprimí konfiansa den biktoria. 'E enmienda no ta ta vali,' el ta di. 'Si e proyektu pasa komo ta sta, parehan homoseksual ta tene akseso a ambos kasamentu i asosiasashon sivil—pero parehan opuesto seksual ta tene solamente kasamentu. E no ta just pa parehan ku ta tin relashonnan amoroso i stabile ku no ta desé bini kasá pero si ta busca reconocimentu legal i protekshon.' E enmienda nôvo di gobièrno, presentá ayer, ta prometí un reseña. Ministri di Kultura Maria Miller, responsabel pa igualdad, ta di: 'E Proyektu di Kasamentu Igual ta pa estendí kasamentu pa parehan homoseksual. Preguntanan ta salí si nos ta ta estendí asosiasashon sivil pa parehan opuesto seksual. Ta ta opinionanan fuerte pa ambas lados, i nos ta skucha. Nos ta ofresí e Kamara e oportunidat pa fá un reseña—no pa lezislá sin evidensia sufisiente.' Sòlo tres dia antis, Miller ta rechazá estendí asosiasashon sivil pa parehan heteroseksual totalmenti, diendo na komité parlaméntario di drenan human: 'Nos no ta sentí ku ta nesesidat ó requerimentu pa abrí asosiasashon sivil pa parehan opuesto seksual—porque e opción ya ta ta aki: kasamentu.' Kampanista di drenan homoseksual Peter Tatchell, ku ta kampaná pa asosiasashon sivil ta ta disponibel pa todó parehan, ta eksprimí desapuntamentu. 'Mientras ku promesa di reseña ta bienvení, ta innesesario,' el ta di. 'Konsulta públiko aña pasá ta mostra ku mayoria di pueblu ta apoiá manteni i estendí asosiasashon sivil. David Cameron i Maria Miller ta di ku ta apoiá igualdad—pero ta negá estendí drenan igual pa parehan heteroseksual. Ta ta inkonsisente.' Un portavoz di Departamentu pa Kultura, Medion i Spurt, ta adi: 'Asosiasashon sivil ta kreado pa un motivu muy espesífiko—pa dá parehan homoseksual akseso a drenan legal ku sosiedat no ta prepará pa dá e akseso pa kasamentu. Ahora ku e tiempu ta propiu pa estendí kasamentu pa parehan homoseksual, ta apropiá pa rekonsiderá e futuro di asosiasashon sivil. Ta ta opinionanan fuerte pa ambas lados—nos ta skucha. Un reseña propi ta permití nos mira e asuntunan den manera pensá i detallá, dándo konsiderasión total pa implikashonnan di kambyanan.'

article_content: Prince Charles isn’t just a royal—he’s a passionate advocate for nature, and Romania has become his second home. He first fell in love with the country during an official trip in 1998, and since then, he’s returned annually, often staying in one of two cozy properties tucked away in Transylvania’s quiet hills. One, the Blue House in Viscri, he bought for just £12,000 in 2006; the other, a rustic lodge near Zalánpatak, offers direct access to wildflower meadows and ancient forests. To help protect these landscapes, Charles backs The European Nature Trust, which turned a classic British double-decker bus into a traveling classroom. Recently, it pulled up outside the British Embassy in Bucharest, filled with Romanian kids shouting excitedly about bears, wolves, and red squirrels. When Charles climbed the stairs, asking what he’d missed, their answers were pure joy. What draws him isn’t just scenery—it’s a way of life. Romania’s countryside still moves to the rhythm of centuries past: horses pull carts, no pesticides touch the soil, and every family makes jam from wild berries. The air smells of thyme, meadows bloom with six times more plant species than Britain’s, and the silence at night is broken only by dog barks and cowbells. He’s so inspired that he’s recreated a piece of Transylvania at his English home, Highgrove, planting wildflower seeds gathered from Romanian hayfields. He even tracked down the elusive bastard toadflax during a walk—and celebrated like a child finding a hidden treasure. Romania’s forests hold more brown bears than any other part of Europe. Wolves and lynx roam freely, keeping deer populations in check and letting the forest heal itself. Scientists say this balance is vital—and Charles agrees. He sees Romania not as backward, but as a living lesson in harmony with nature. Tourists rarely see this Romania. There are no supermarkets, no wind turbines, no formal pavements. Just stone cottages, handwoven textiles, and women selling colorful socks in village squares. The people aren’t waiting for aid—they’re sustaining themselves, generation after generation. Though his wife, the Duchess of Cornwall, hasn’t joined him yet, his sons have. Prince Harry once flew in on a £40 Wizz Air flight to stay with the estate manager. And while modern life creeps closer, Charles fights quietly—not with protests, but with preservation. He rents out his homes so others can experience this world, hoping more will understand what’s at stake. As he puts it: ‘It’s the timelessness that matters.’ For Charles, Romania isn’t a destination—it’s a reminder of how the world could still be.

article_content: When Chancellor George Osborne expanded VAT to include hot takeaway meals like pasties and pies, he didn’t anticipate how deeply it would confuse the very people trying to enforce it. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) was left scrambling—not because of complex tax law, but because no one could agree on what counts as bread. While cold bread escapes VAT entirely—even if it’s warmed in an oven—other baked goods like croissants, scones, and hot-cross buns sit in a gray zone. Are they bread? Or are they luxury snacks? The government has now opened a public consultation to settle the debate, but even retail experts admit they’re baffled. Some bakeries, including Greggs and Subway, argue their hot items aren’t meant to be eaten warm; they’re simply heated for safety or presentation. Greggs, which made over £50 million in profit each year from 2010 to 2011 and operates nearly 1,500 stores across Britain, has threatened legal action if HMRC labels its products as taxable 'hot food'. Meanwhile, the policy is expected to bring in £125 million this year and £350 million annually by 2016—but at a cost: a 90p sausage roll will now cost £1.08, and a £1.49 pasty will jump to £1.79. Critics say the distinction is arbitrary, especially when a buttery croissant might be taxed while a plain roll isn’t. The whole situation has turned a simple tax update into a national identity crisis: What even is bread?

article_content: Brazil’s coach Luiz Felipe Scolari has called on his players and the nation to look beyond the crushing 7-1 defeat to Germany in the World Cup semi-final. While the fallout continues to dominate headlines, Scolari insists the focus must shift to the upcoming third-place playoff against the Netherlands. His tenure as head coach appears likely to end after the tournament, following Brazil’s worst defeat since a 6-0 loss to Uruguay in 1920. Speaking at a press conference in Teresópolis, Scolari acknowledged the loss will define his legacy but stressed the importance of finishing the tournament with pride. 'We have an obligation to move forward and aim for our next goal — the match for third place in Brasília,' he said. 'It’s a smaller dream than we hoped for, but we must honor the national shirt.' He added that the tournament wasn’t entirely negative: 'We had a bad defeat, but we also reached the semi-finals for the first time since 2002.' Regarding his future, Scolari confirmed his contract with the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) expires after the third-place match, saying a discussion will follow. 'We’ll submit a full report to the CBF board detailing what we did well and where we fell short — the rest depends on their direction.' He emphasized that life must go on for both players and staff: 'You can't end the lives of players because of one result.' His assistant, Carlos Alberto Parreira, echoed the need for systemic change, praising Germany’s superior football infrastructure. 'They have world-class training centers for players and coaches — the results speak for themselves,' Parreira said. 'Now is the time to rethink, revise, and invest in youth development, club structures, and professional training. Brazil must rebuild from the ground up.'

'Despues di e Mundial nos ta presentá un rapòrtu pa e junta di CBF, ku ta vín e bín i e mal ku nos ta fá, i despues ta dependí di e direkshon. 'Nan ta nengun pensamentu pa mi testa hodi. Nos ta sigui ku nos vida, e spelmennan también ta sigui komo ganadornan, i nos ta tin ku sigui — no ta posibel pa ta tèrminá e vida di e spelmennan pa eza.' 'Historia ta tin ku registrá ku Brasil, pa e primé vez desde 2002, ta bini pa e semifinal.' Asistente di Scolari, Carlos Alberto Parreira, a dí ku e ora ta pa reevaluá e fútbol brasileron despues di akmé ku Alemania ta mihor avanzá na to aspektu di e juego. 'E ta tin múltiplu sentros di entrenamentu pa atletanan, tambe pa entrenadornan, i e rezultá ta vín akí,' el a dí. 'Fútbol alemán ta e base perfekto i nos ta tin un oportunidat pa re pensar, revisá i invertí na entrenamentu mejor pa atletanan. 'Nos ta tin ku mehorá i enfoká na entrenamentu di atletanan di e klubnan i dá atensión total pa eza, dá buenas struktura i entrená profesionalnan bon.'

article_content: Though it takes place in a prison where meals might include something as absurd as a 'tampon sandwich,' 'Orange Is the New Black' isn’t just gritty drama — it’s smart, layered storytelling. The show casually drops references to Shakespeare, Joyce, and Robert Frost, turning everyday moments into profound reflections. In Season 2, Officer Fischer marvels at the inmates’ lives, comparing them to Dickens — and she’s not wrong. Like Dickens, the series paints a vivid, unsparing portrait of broken systems through unforgettable, oddly named characters whose quirks reveal deeper truths. We get to know Poussey, Taystee, and Crazy Eyes more intimately this season, especially as Vee enters their world, forcing painful choices and revealing hidden vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, Piper’s journey evolves: she’s no longer the idealistic, Whole Foods-shopping liberal. When she’s faced with testifying against a drug kingpin to protect Alex, she confronts her own moral ambiguity, declaring herself a 'lone wolf.' The show also skewers white privilege brilliantly — like when Piper sighs that she forgot what it was like to waste time waiting in line for a trendy bagnut. Yet amid the chaos, there’s tenderness: Vee saves cake for Crazy Eyes; Poussey helps Taystee fix her skirt for Career Day; and Nicky reminds Piper she’s 'one Cheerio in the bulk box of life' — but damn, she tickles. It’s not classic literature, but it’s deeply human. And that’s why it earns an A.

E serie ta kousa referensianan a Shakespeare, Joyce, i Robert Frost, transformando momentanan di dia a dia pa reflexionanan profundo. Na tempada 2, Ofisial Fischer ta maravillá pa vida di prisioneranan, komparandoló ku Dickens — i e ta no mal. Komò Dickens, e serie ta pintá un retrato vívido i sin compasión di sistemanan rotu atraves di karaktenan inolvidabel, kon nomberenan raro ku karkteristikunan lor ta revelá verdadanan mas profundo. Nos ta konosé Poussey, Taystee, i Crazy Eyes mas intimo na tempada aki, spesialmente ku Vee ta entra na mundu lor, forzándo ele skolhas doloroso i revelándo vulnerabilidatnan escondí. Mientrás, e jerni di Piper ta evolusioná: e no ta mas e liberal idealista ku ta kompa na Whole Foods. Ku e ta fasé e desizion si ta testifiká kontre un jefe di droga pa proteje Alex, e ta konfrontá su ambiguidat moral, declarándo si mesm ‘un lobo solitario.’ E serie ta tira satira briljante pa privilegio blancho — komo ku Piper ta suspirá ku e ta olvidá kua ta e senso di perdí tempu na fila pa un bagnut modérno. Pero amedas e kahos, ta bini ternura: Vee ta salba un trok di torta pa Crazy Eyes; Poussey ta ajuda Taystee pa konsertá su falda pa Career Day; i Nicky ta recordá Piper ku e ta ‘un Cheerio na la caja di masa’ — pero mierda, e ta taiká mi. E no ta literatura klásiko, pero e ta profundamente humano. I por eso e ta meresí un A.

article_content: Flight restrictions over national parks, military bases, and airports are clearly defined and strictly enforced. But as drones become more common, homeowners and businesses are growing increasingly worried about unauthorized flights over their private property. To address these concerns, Ben Marcus, a pilot from California, has partnered with leading drone manufacturers to create NoFlyZone.org — a global database that allows property owners to register no-fly zones above their homes and offices. To add a zone, users enter their property’s location, name, and email address for verification. The system converts this information into precise latitude and longitude coordinates, along with boundary points that outline the full extent of the property. For the first registered property, no proof of ownership is required. However, for any additional properties, users must submit a form of identification or a recent utility bill. Once verified, the data is sent to participating drone manufacturers and integrated into their drones’ no-fly databases. Many modern drones are programmed to automatically avoid these registered zones during flight. If someone living near a registered property wants to fly their own drone, they must prove residency. NoFlyZone will temporarily unblock the airspace upon request, and property owners can unblock their own zones at any time. At launch, NoFlyZone partnered with seven major drone makers: Horizon Hobby, Yuneec, Hexo+, PixiPath, Ehang (maker of the Ghost drone), Drone Deploy, and RCFlyMaps. These companies have pledged to honor registered zones — though they are not legally required to do so. Marcus recommends that each no-fly zone cover a 500-foot (152-meter) radius around the property, but the exact size may vary by manufacturer. Legally, drones remain prohibited from flying over national parks, military installations, and within a five-mile (8-kilometer) radius of medium and large airports. Commercial drones face even stricter regulations. ‘Evolving technology allows drones to positively impact daily life — but they can also threaten privacy and safety,’ said Marcus. ‘NoFlyZone.org gives people a way to reclaim control over their airspace.’ While government agencies like the FAA work to establish comprehensive drone laws, manufacturers and operators are taking proactive steps to self-regulate and minimize harm. Database updates are sent to partners once a month. New drones produced after each update include the latest no-fly zones. Existing drones won’t be updated automatically — meaning it may take time for all in-service units to reflect new registrations. Looking ahead, Marcus plans to enable real-time updates via internet-connected drones, allowing privacy settings to be pushed directly to devices as soon as changes are made.

Pa aña un zona, usuario ta tuma su lokashon, nomber i e-mail pa verifikashon. Sisteman ta konbertí es informashon na koordinadanan di latitud i longitud, ku ta marká e bordanan di propiedade. Pa primèr propiedade, ta no pedí pruèba di residensia. Pero pa otro propiedade, usuario ta tení ku presentá un identifikashon o bil di utilidat. Despues di verifikashon, datanan ta mandá pa fabricante di drone i ta integrá na bista di no-vooch di drone. Muncha drone moderno ta programá pa evitá es zonanan registrá. Si un persona ku ta vivi riba un propiedade registrá ta bini pa vooch su drone, el ta tení ku probar residensia. NoFlyZone ta desblokeá e espasio aèrio temporalmente, i propietario ta pòdes desblokeá su propiedade ku ta bini. Al lansamentu, NoFlyZone ta konsultá ku siete fabricante grandi: Horizon Hobby, Yuneec, Hexo+, PixiPath, Ehang (fabricante di e Ghost), Drone Deploy i RCFlyMaps. Es kompanianan ta prometí pa respetá zonanan registrá — pero ta no obligashon legal. Marcus ta rekomentá ku cada zona di no-vooch ta kubre un radia di 500-pi (152-metro) riba propiedade, pero e tamanyo ta pòdes kambia segun fabricante. Legalmenti, drone ta prohibí pa vooch riba parknan nasional, instalashonan militar, i den un radia di 5 milla (8 km) di aeroportu grandi. Drone komersial ta tené regulashonan mas estricto. ‘Teknolojia ku ta evolushoná ta permití ku drone ta tene un efektu positivo na vida di dia a dia — pero ta tambe pòdes amenasa privasía i sekuridat,’ di Marcus. ‘NoFlyZone.org ta ofresé pa personanan un manerá pa rekupera kontrol di e espasio aèrio riba su propiedade.’ Mientras agensianan gobièrnamental komo FAA ta trabá pa kria regulashonan kompletu pa drone, fabricante i operador ta toma pasu proaktivo pa auto-regulá i minimizá konsekwenxia negativo. Aktualizashonan di bista ta mandá pa partner un vezen pa mes. Drone nèw ku ta producí despues di es aktualizashon ta inklui e zonanan mas reciente. Drone ku ta bini ta no aktualizá automaticamente — ku ta signifika ku ta pòdes tuma tempu pa toto e drone di serbisu ta refleja registrashonan nèw. Pa e futuro, Marcus ta planea pa habilitá aktualizashonan en tiempu real ku drone ta konektá pa internet, permití ku setting di privasía ta push directamente pa drone ku ta bini.
